prompt: When does Compute Engine run a machine's startup script?
hint: Not only at creation.

choices.text: Once, the first time the machine is created
choices.why: That is the common belief; the guest environment runs it at every boot.

choices.text: Whenever its metadata changes, without a reboot
choices.why: A change takes effect at the next boot, or when you run the script runner by hand.

choices.text: On every boot, as root
choices.why: Right. Which is why the script must be safe to run twice.

choices.text: Only when the machine is started from a stopped state, as an unprivileged user
choices.why: It runs at every boot, and as root.

prompt: A public image runs its startup script; a custom image built from scratch boots and ignores it. What is the likely cause?
hint: Who reads the startup-script key?

choices.text: No guest environment on the image to run it
choices.why: Right. Google runs nothing; the guest environment on the machine does.

choices.text: Custom images are not allowed startup scripts
choices.why: They are; something on the machine has to run them.

choices.text: The metadata key must be startup-script-url for custom images
choices.why: Either key works when the guest environment is present.

choices.text: The script is too long for the metadata server
choices.why: Length would give an error at creation, not a silent skip.

prompt: Run on the laptop, startup.sh stopped with curl: (6) and status 6. Without -sSf and set -euo pipefail, what would it have done?
hint: What is in ENV when curl fails quietly?

choices.text: Stopped anyway, because bash exits on the first error
choices.why: bash carries on after a failed command unless told otherwise.

choices.text: Asked for the zone again until the server answered
choices.why: Nothing in the script retries.

choices.text: Read the values from the Terraform state instead
choices.why: The script knows nothing about Terraform.

choices.text: Written a page with empty values and exited 0
choices.why: Right. A silent failure nobody finds until a customer does.

prompt: The script is set with metadata_startup_script, and someone fixes a typo in it. What happens at the next apply, according to the provider's documentation?
hint: That attribute is special among the ways to set a script.

choices.text: The metadata changes in place and the script runs at the next boot
choices.why: That is what the startup-script key inside metadata does.

choices.text: The instance is destroyed and a new one created
choices.why: Right. That attribute forces replacement; the metadata key updates in place.

choices.text: Nothing until somebody runs the script runner on the machine
choices.why: Terraform does act on the change, and drastically.

choices.text: The apply fails, because a running machine's script is locked
choices.why: Nothing locks it; the provider plans a replacement.

prompt: A startup script's output can be read from outside the machine on its ___ console, even when SSH is broken.
hint: A port, not a screen.

prompt: Which header must every request to the metadata server carry?
hint: It names whose metadata this is.

choices.text: Authorization: Bearer with the instance token
choices.why: The token is what you ask for; you cannot need it to ask.

choices.text: X-Forwarded-For with the machine's address
choices.why: A request carrying that header is refused.

choices.text: Metadata-Flavor: Google
choices.why: Right. Without it the server answers 403.

choices.text: X-Goog-Project with the project id
choices.why: No such header is required; the machine already belongs to a project.

prompt: Why does the metadata server refuse requests that carry X-Forwarded-For?
hint: Who adds that header?

choices.text: A proxy tricked into forwarding a request adds it on the way
choices.why: Right. It closes the reverse-proxy route to the token.

choices.text: Because the header would reveal the machine's internal address
choices.why: The server is inside the host; revealing addresses is not the concern.

choices.text: Because load balancers in front of the machine send it
choices.why: A load balancer cannot reach the metadata address at all.

choices.text: Because the header makes responses too large to cache
choices.why: Caching has nothing to do with it.

prompt: An attacker gets a shell on web-1. What does the Metadata-Flavor header do to stop them taking the service account's token?
hint: A filter for forged fetches, or a lock?

choices.text: It blocks requests from interactive sessions
choices.why: The server cannot tell a shell from a service.

choices.text: It requires the request to come from the guest environment
choices.why: Any process on the machine may ask.

choices.text: It limits the token to read-only scopes for shells
choices.why: Scopes are set per instance, not per caller.

choices.text: Nothing: a shell sends the header like any program
choices.why: Right. That is why the token should be worth as little as possible.

prompt: A script must react when the attribute shop-env changes, without polling every few seconds. What does the metadata server offer?
hint: A query parameter.

choices.text: ?recursive=true, which streams every change
choices.why: recursive returns a whole tree at once; it does not wait.

choices.text: ?wait_for_change=true
choices.why: Right. The guest environment uses it for new SSH keys.

choices.text: A Pub/Sub topic the server publishes changes to
choices.why: The metadata server publishes nothing.

choices.text: A webhook URL set in the instance metadata
choices.why: There is no such webhook.

prompt: Which of these belong in instance metadata? Choose all that apply.
hint: Who can read metadata?

choices.text: The environment name, staging
choices.why: Right; nobody is hurt by reading it.

choices.text: The database password
choices.why: Every process and every viewer of the instance reads metadata; use Secret Manager.

choices.text: The startup script itself
choices.why: Right, as long as no secret is written inside it.

choices.text: A service account's JSON key
choices.why: That is the worst of both: a secret, and one that never expires.

prompt: How long does the token the metadata server hands out live?
hint: Short-lived, and replaced.

choices.text: Until the machine is deleted
choices.why: That would be a key file's weakness.

choices.text: Ninety days, like a rotated key
choices.why: Tokens are far shorter than key rotation periods.

choices.text: About an hour, renewed before it expires
choices.why: Right. Your code never sees a key.

choices.text: One request; each call needs a fresh one
choices.why: A token is reused until it nears expiry.

prompt: adc.py ran with GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS pointing at a missing file and said "File ... was not found." Why did it not go on to try the metadata server?
hint: What does that variable mean to the library?

choices.text: The variable names one file, and only that file is used
choices.why: Right. It is the first step of the order and it does not fall through.

choices.text: The metadata server was tried first and had already failed
choices.why: It comes last in the order, not first.

choices.text: A missing file is treated as a revoked account
choices.why: Nothing about the account was checked.

choices.text: The run happened too fast for the network to come up
choices.why: Timing is not why; the order is.

prompt: Put the places Application Default Credentials looks in the order it tries them.
hint: The explicit choice first, the machine last.
items: The file gcloud auth application-default login writes
trap: The metadata server is last, which is why the laptop spent three seconds on it before giving up.

prompt: Why create shop-web instead of using the Compute Engine default service account?
hint: What did the default account get in older projects?

choices.text: The default account cannot be attached to E2 machines
choices.why: It can be attached to any machine.

choices.text: The default account's tokens never expire, unlike a dedicated account's
choices.why: Its tokens expire like any other.

choices.text: Terraform cannot read the default account's email
choices.why: That is not the reason; the risk is its roles.

choices.text: Old defaults hold Editor; a dedicated one holds only what it needs
choices.why: Right. A stolen token then reads what a web server reads, nothing more.

prompt: In the capture, how many seconds (real) did adc.py take to give up on a laptop with no metadata server? Answer to one decimal.
hint: Read the real line of time.

prompt: A call from the machine succeeds only when what holds?
hint: Two checks.

choices.text: The scope covers the API, whatever the roles
choices.why: Roles are checked too.

choices.text: The scope covers the API and a role covers the action
choices.why: Right. Each can fail alone.

choices.text: A role covers the action, whatever the scope
choices.why: A narrow scope blocks it even with the role.

choices.text: The machine is in the same zone as the resource
choices.why: Location does not authorise anything.

prompt: In the plan the alias storage-ro became https://www.googleapis.com/auth/devstorage.___.
hint: Read only.

prompt: What does Google recommend for a machine's scopes?
hint: Which of the two checks can say "this bucket"?

choices.text: The narrowest scopes possible, and no IAM roles at all
choices.why: Without roles the account can do nothing.

choices.text: No scopes, so the metadata server issues no token
choices.why: Then the machine has no use for its account.

choices.text: cloud-platform, with IAM roles deciding access
choices.why: Right. Roles are precise and change without touching the machine.

choices.text: A different scope per process on the machine
choices.why: Scopes are set per instance.

prompt: A team removes a role from shop-web after a leak, and an hour-old token from web-1 is still working minutes later against an API that role covered. What explains it, and what cuts it off faster?
hint: Role changes propagate; tokens live until they expire.

choices.text: Propagation takes a while; disabling the service account cuts faster
choices.why: Right. A disabled account's credentials are refused.

choices.text: The role was cached on the machine; reboot it
choices.why: Roles are checked by the API, not cached on the machine.

choices.text: Scopes override roles, so change the machine's scopes instead
choices.why: Changing scopes needs a stop and does not touch issued tokens.

choices.text: Metadata tokens ignore IAM; delete the instance
choices.why: Every call is checked against IAM.

prompt: Terraform refuses to change the scopes of a running web-1. What makes the change possible?
hint: The machine has to stop for it.

choices.text: Running terraform apply twice
choices.why: Repetition does not change what the API requires.

choices.text: Moving the scopes into metadata
choices.why: Scopes are not metadata values.

choices.text: Detaching the service account first
choices.why: That is itself a change needing a stop.

choices.text: allow_stopping_for_update = true
choices.why: Right. The change needs a stopped instance.

prompt: Put what happens when web-1 boots in order.
hint: The script needs the metadata server and the guest environment.
items: The guest environment starts on the machine
It reads the startup-script key from the metadata server
The script asks the metadata server for shop-env and the zone
nginx serves the page the script wrote
trap: The script cannot ask anything before the guest environment has fetched and started it.

prompt: Match each metadata path to what it returns.
hint: instance/ is this machine, project/ is everyone's.

pairs.right: Where Compute Engine placed the machine
A value you set on this machine

prompt: A web server fetches images from URLs that users type. Which change limits the damage if that feature is abused to reach the metadata server?
hint: Two layers: the filter, and what the token is worth.

choices.text: Moving shop-env out of instance metadata
choices.why: The token is the prize, not the environment name.

choices.text: A dedicated service account holding only the web server's roles
choices.why: Right. Even if a fetch got through, the token would be worth little.

choices.text: Turning off OS Login on the machine
choices.why: OS Login is about SSH, not the metadata server.

choices.text: Using startup-script-url instead of the startup-script key
choices.why: Where the script lives does not protect the token.

prompt: In section 03's capture, what exit status did curl give for the metadata address on this laptop?
hint: curl numbers its failures.

prompt: Google's libraries find credentials through Application ___ Credentials, the same search on a laptop and on a machine.
hint: The credentials used when nothing else is said.
